arXiv:2609.26464v1 [math.GR] 22 Sep 2026

Refining invariants of finite groups with class functions

Christopher A. Schroeder Address: HUN-REN Alfréd Rényi Institute of Mathematics, Reáltanoda utca 13-15, H-1053 Budapest, Hungary Email address: schroeder.chris@renyi.hu
Date: September 22, 2026
Abstract.

Many numerical invariants of a finite group arise as the multiplicity of the trivial character in a naturally associated class function, and the remaining multiplicities carry finer structural information. For the number of conjugacy classes of elements whose order involves only a chosen set of primes, the natural such class function is a generalized character interpolating between the classical conjugating character and the regular character. We prove that it is a character in two important general cases, obtained independently by Robinson, and we rule out a family of groups and characters in which, we argue, a counterexample would be most likely to arise. Furthermore, we characterize when these class functions are compatible with passing to a subgroup and thereby sharpen a theorem of Sangroniz. The analogous class function for real elements is shown to always give a character. Finally, we give a dual construction that, together with the recently proved McKay Conjecture, yields a best-possible criterion for a finite group to have an abelian Sylow pp-subgroup.

1. Introduction

There is a long history of using invariants to unravel the structure of mathematical objects. By a group invariant we mean a function assigning to each finite group GG a complex number IGI_{G} such that IG=IHI_{G}=I_{H} whenever G≅HG\cong H. As nonisomorphic groups could have the same value of an invariant, one would often like to refine, or strengthen, an invariant to obtain more detailed information about group structure. We take up this problem here in the following way: Given an invariant IGI_{G}, we seek a complex-valued class function 𝐈G:G→ℂ\mathbf{I}_{G}:G\rightarrow\mathbb{C} such that, in a chosen orthonormal basis {e1,…,en}\{e_{1},\dots,e_{n}\} of the space of class functions, the class function 𝐈G\mathbf{I}_{G} has our invariant IGI_{G} as the weight [𝐈G,e1][\mathbf{I}_{G},e_{1}] of its fundamental component e1e_{1}. Such a class function always exists, and the construction need not be unique; indeed, 𝐈G=IG​e1\mathbf{I}_{G}=I_{G}\,e_{1} is a trivial way to construct such a class function. However, even trivial constructions can be interesting, as we will see in Example 2.8. In general, our goal is to find a natural, interesting or useful class function 𝐈G\mathbf{I}_{G} satisfying IG=[𝐈G,e1]I_{G}=[\mathbf{I}_{G},e_{1}].

The idea has an analogy in Fourier analysis and music: If our group GG were a tuned drum, then 𝐈G\mathbf{I}_{G} captures its frequency spectrum when struck, where IG=[𝐈G,e1]I_{G}=[\mathbf{I}_{G},e_{1}] is the weight of the fundamental frequency and the multiplicities IGei:=[𝐈G,ei]I_{G}^{e_{i}}:=[\mathbf{I}_{G},e_{i}] (i>1i>1) are the weights of the “higher harmonics”. Seen in this light, one might hope that 𝐈G\mathbf{I}_{G} can discriminate between groups that have the same value of IGI_{G} in the same way that some musical instruments, such as a trumpet and a cornet, have the same fundamental frequency but can be distinguished by their distributions of higher frequencies, their so-called timbre.

Given such a class function 𝐈G\mathbf{I}_{G}, some natural questions immediately arise:

  1. item (1)(1)

    Is 𝐈G\mathbf{I}_{G} a (generalized) character? Does there exist some c∈ℂc\in\mathbb{C} such that c​𝐈Gc\mathbf{I}_{G} is a (generalized) character?

  2. item (2)(2)

    What can we say about the multiplicities IGeiI_{G}^{e_{i}} (i>1i>1)? For example, when are they nonzero? If they are integers, do they encode any interesting combinatorial information?

  3. item (3)(3)

    What group structure does 𝐈G\mathbf{I}_{G} capture? For example, what is the relationship between a group GG and a subgroup H≤GH\leq G if 𝐈G=(𝐈H)G\mathbf{I}_{G}=(\mathbf{I}_{H})^{G}? Note that if we choose e1e_{1} to be the trivial character 1G1_{G}, then the condition that 𝐈G=(𝐈H)G\mathbf{I}_{G}=(\mathbf{I}_{H})^{G} in Question 3 is a true refinement of IG=IHI_{G}=I_{H} since we have by Frobenius reciprocity that

    IG=[𝐈G,1G]=[(𝐈H)G,1G]=[𝐈H,1H]=IH.\displaystyle I_{G}=[\mathbf{I}_{G},1_{G}]=[(\mathbf{I}_{H})^{G},1_{G}]=[\mathbf{I}_{H},1_{H}]=I_{H}.

    We will address Questions (1)–(3) for some invariants IGI_{G} and refining class functions 𝐈G\mathbf{I}_{G} in this note.

    The layout of the paper is as follows. In Section 2, we define two natural bases for the space of complex class functions on a group. We then describe some previous results from the literature that can be recast in the class function language. In Sections 3–4, we define some new class functions that refine invariants related to conjugacy classes of a finite group, and we address Questions (1)–(3) above for these class functions. Finally, in Section 5, we consider a dual construction and prove a best-possible criterion for a finite group to have an abelian Sylow pp-subgroup using an invariant that is naturally suggested by the construction.

    Notation. Our notation is standard. All groups in this paper are finite. Let GG be a group. For each element x∈Gx\in G, we denote by xG={xg∣g∈G}x^{G}=\{x^{g}\mid g\in G\} its GG-conjugacy class. The collection of conjugacy classes is denoted by Cl⁡(G)\mathrm{Cl}(G), and their number is k⁡(G)k(G). We let xi∈Gx_{i}\in G for i=1,…,k⁡(G)i=1,\dots,k(G) be representatives for the GG-conjugacy classes. The collection of irreducible complex characters of GG is denoted Irr⁡(G)\mathrm{Irr}(G). It is known that k⁡(G)=|Irr⁡(G)|k(G)=|\mathrm{Irr}(G)|. Let χ1\chi_{1} be the trivial character, which we often denote as 1G1_{G}. The irreducible characters are orthonormal with respect to the inner product [χi,χj]=(1/|G|)​∑g∈Gχi​(g)​χj​(g)¯[\chi_{i},\chi_{j}]=(1/|G|)\sum_{g\in G}\chi_{i}(g)\overline{\chi_{j}(g)}. Let cf⁡(G)\mathrm{cf}(G) be the vector space of complex-valued class functions on GG. Now let pp be a prime. The collection of GG-conjugacy classes consisting of elements of order coprime to pp, also called p′p^{\prime}-elements or pp-regular elements, is denoted by Clp′​(G)\mathrm{Cl}_{p^{\prime}}(G). The number of pp-regular conjugacy classes of GG is kp′​(G)=|Clp′​(G)|k_{p^{\prime}}(G)=|\mathrm{Cl}_{p^{\prime}}(G)|. Let IBrp​(G)\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(G) be the irreducible pp-Brauer characters of GG. Now let π\pi be a collection of primes. Let Gπ⊆GG_{\pi}\subseteq G denote the set of π\pi-elements of GG, let Clπ​(G)\mathrm{Cl}_{\pi}(G) denote the collection of GG-conjugacy classes of π\pi-elements, let |G|π|G|_{\pi} denote the π\pi-part of the integer |G||G|, and let kπ​(G)k_{\pi}(G) be the number of π\pi-conjugacy classes of GG.

    2. Examples

    In this section, we give some examples from the literature that can be formulated using the class function language described in the introduction. In our first collection of examples, we choose a basis for the space cf⁡(G)\mathrm{cf}(G) of complex class functions on a finite group GG consisting of the irreducible ordinary characters Irr⁡(G)\mathrm{Irr}(G).

    Example 2.1.

    (Element orders.) The invariant IG=∑g∈G|g|I_{G}=\sum_{g\in G}|g| summing the element orders has been much studied from a group theoretical point of view; see [1, 2, 17, 18, 29, 30, 44, 45] and the references therein. Moretó studied the class function defined by 𝐈G​(g)=|G|​|g|\mathbf{I}_{G}(g)=|G||g| for all g∈Gg\in G in [36], noting that IG=[𝐈G,1G]I_{G}=[\mathbf{I}_{G},1_{G}]. Moretó proved, among other things, that 𝐈G\mathbf{I}_{G} is a generalized character.

    The closely related invariant IG=(1/|G|)​∑g∈G|g|I_{G}=(1/|G|)\sum_{g\in G}|g| calculating the average element order has also been much studied; see [18, 25, 28, 31]. The class function defined by 𝐈G​(g)=|g|\mathbf{I}_{G}(g)=|g| satisfies IG=[𝐈G,1G]I_{G}=[\mathbf{I}_{G},1_{G}]. Moretó showed that the smallest positive integer mm such that m​𝐈Gm\mathbf{I}_{G} is a generalized character is m=|G|m=|G|.

    Example 2.2.

    (Conjugacy classes.) If IG=k⁡(G)I_{G}=k(G), the number of conjugacy classes of GG, then the class function defined by 𝐈G​(g)=|𝐂G​(g)|\mathbf{I}_{G}(g)=|\mathbf{C}_{G}(g)| for all g∈Gg\in G satisfies IG=[𝐈G,1G]I_{G}=[\mathbf{I}_{G},1_{G}]. This class function is the character, often denoted ΠG\Pi_{G}, of the so-called conjugating representation, which is the linear representation obtained by letting GG act by conjugation on its group algebra ℂ​G\mathbb{C}G. The study of the constituents of the conjugating representation has a long history; see [15, 16] and the references therein.

    The closely related invariant IG=k⁡(G)/|G|I_{G}=k(G)/|G| then arises via the class function 𝐈G​(g)=|𝐂G​(g)|/|G|\mathbf{I}_{G}(g)=|\mathbf{C}_{G}(g)|/|G|. It has been pointed out by many authors that the invariant d⁡(G)=k⁡(G)/|G|d(G)=k(G)/|G| is equal to the probability that two randomly chosen elements of GG commute; see [10, 14, 26, 27]. Many studies have shown that this invariant, often called the commuting probability or commutativity degree, encodes important structural information about the group; see [8, 13, 14, 32] and the references therein. For example, Gustafson proved in [14] that if d⁡(G)>5/8d(G)>5/8, then GG is abelian.

    Example 2.3.

    (Permutation characters.) The last example can be put in a more general context. Note that if GG acts on a finite set Ω\Omega and 𝐈G\mathbf{I}_{G} is the permutation character, then 𝐈G​(g)=|FixΩ​(g)|\mathbf{I}_{G}(g)=|\mathrm{Fix}_{\Omega}(g)|, and so by Burnside’s counting theorem

    IG={# of G-orbits on Ω}=1|G|​∑g∈G|FixΩ​(g)|=[𝐈G,1G].\displaystyle I_{G}=\{\text{\# of $G$-orbits on $\Omega$}\}=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}|\mathrm{Fix}_{\Omega}(g)|=[\mathbf{I}_{G},1_{G}].

    Example 2.2 arises from this construction with GG acting on Ω=G\Omega=G by conjugation.

    Now let AA be any finitely-generated group, and let GG act on Ω=Hom⁡(A,G)\Omega=\mathrm{Hom}(A,G) by post-composition with conjugation, i.e. g⋅ϕ=g​ϕ​(−)​g−1g\cdot\phi=g\phi(-)g^{-1}. Then |FixΩ​(g)|=|Hom⁡(A,𝐂G​(g))||\mathrm{Fix}_{\Omega}(g)|=|\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbf{C}_{G}(g))|, and so the class function defined by 𝐈G​(g)=|Hom⁡(A,𝐂G​(g))|\mathbf{I}_{G}(g)=|\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbf{C}_{G}(g))| for all g∈Gg\in G has the associated invariant

    IG=[𝐈G,1G]={# of G-orbits on Hom⁡(A,G)}.\displaystyle I_{G}=[\mathbf{I}_{G},1_{G}]=\{\text{\# of $G$-orbits on $\mathrm{Hom}(A,G)$}\}.

    This gives rise to more examples:

    1. (1)

      If A=ℤA=\mathbb{Z}, then Hom⁡(A,G)≅G\mathrm{Hom}(A,G)\cong G, Hom⁡(A,𝐂G​(g))≅𝐂G​(g)\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbf{C}_{G}(g))\cong\mathbf{C}_{G}(g), and we recover IG=k⁡(G)I_{G}=k(G) and 𝐈G​(g)=|𝐂G​(g)|\mathbf{I}_{G}(g)=|\mathbf{C}_{G}(g)| for all g∈Gg\in G from Example 2.2.

    2. (2)

      If A=FnA=F_{n} (the free group on nn generators), then Hom⁡(A,G)≅Gn\mathrm{Hom}(A,G)\cong G^{n}, 𝐈G​(g)=|𝐂G​(g)|n\mathbf{I}_{G}(g)=|\mathbf{C}_{G}(g)|^{n} and IGI_{G} is the number of conjugacy classes of nn-tuples under simultaneous conjugation.

    3. (3)

      If A=ℤnA=\mathbb{Z}^{n}, then Hom⁡(A,G)\mathrm{Hom}(A,G) is the set of pairwise-commuting nn-tuples in GG, and GG acts on these tuples by simultaneous conjugation. So IGI_{G} is the number of conjugacy classes of nn-tuples with pairwise-commuting elements.

    The invariant in (3) was considered by Levit and Shwartz in their investigations of the so-called “higher commutativity” [33, 34]. Commuting nn-tuples were also considered by Erdős and Straus [9].

    Example 2.4.

    (Adams operations.) Given an irreducible character χ∈Irr⁡(G)\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(G) of a finite group GG, the class function 𝐈χ,G=χ(2)\mathbf{I}_{\chi,G}=\chi^{(2)} defined by χ(2)​(g)=χ⁡(g2)\chi^{(2)}(g)=\chi(g^{2}) for all g∈Gg\in G gives rise to the so-called Frobenius–Schur indicator of χ\chi, Iχ,G=[𝐈χ,G,1G]=(1/|G|)​∑g∈Gχ⁡(g2)I_{\chi,G}=[\mathbf{I}_{\chi,G},1_{G}]=(1/|G|)\sum_{g\in G}\chi(g^{2}). See [22, Chapter 4] for more information about this classical topic.

    Recently, Boltje, Kleshchev, Navarro and Tiep proved a reduction of the Feit Conjecture to a local problem on finite simple groups [3]. The authors also formulated a stronger form of the conjecture [3, Conjecture E] which is connected to an integer-valued invariant S⁡(G,χ,n)S(G,\chi,n) studied by Boltje and Navarro in [4], where GG is a finite group, χ∈Irr⁡(G)\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(G) and nn is a positive integer. One way to construct this invariant is as the multiplicity of the trivial character in a generalized character constructed from a particular integral linear combination of Adams operations Ψk​(χ)\Psi^{k}(\chi) of χ\chi, where Ψk​(χ)​(g)=χ⁡(gk)\Psi^{k}(\chi)(g)=\chi(g^{k}) for all g∈Gg\in G [4, Theorem B]. Note that Ψ2​(χ)=χ(2)\Psi^{2}(\chi)=\chi^{(2)} from the last paragraph.

    Example 2.5.

    (An example of Frobenius.) Frobenius considered the following example, which is described in [21, V.19.13–V.19.14]. Let KK be a conjugacy class of a finite group GG, let nn be a divisor of |G||G|, and let tt be the number of elements g∈Gg\in G such that gn∈Kg^{n}\in K. The rational number IG=t/nI_{G}=t/n is an invariant of the group GG. Now, if we define the class function 𝐈G\mathbf{I}_{G} on GG by 𝐈G​(g)=|G|/n\mathbf{I}_{G}(g)=|G|/n if gn∈Kg^{n}\in K and 00 otherwise, then we have

    [𝐈G,1G]=1|G|​∑g∈G𝐈G​(g)=tn=IG.\displaystyle[\mathbf{I}_{G},1_{G}]=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\mathbf{I}_{G}(g)=\frac{t}{n}=I_{G}.

    In fact, the class function perspective gives interesting information about the invariant IGI_{G} in this case: Our class function 𝐈G\mathbf{I}_{G} can be expressed as a linear combination of irreducible characters with coefficients in ℂ\mathbb{C}. However, it is shown in [21, Theorem V.19.13] that the coefficients are actually algebraic integers lying in ℤ⁡[ϵ]\mathbb{Z}[\epsilon], where ϵ\epsilon is a primitive |G||G|-th root of unity. In particular, the coefficient [𝐈G,1G]=IG[\mathbf{I}_{G},1_{G}]=I_{G} is an algebraic integer. So, IGI_{G} is a rational number and an algebraic integer, which implies that IGI_{G} is an integer. This is not at all obvious from the definition.

    The next example will be one of the main concerns of this paper. We will consider it in detail in Sections 3 and 4.

    Example 2.6.

    (“Local” conjugating character.) There has been much interest in a so-called “π\pi-local” version of the invariant d⁡(G)d(G) from Example 2.2; the invariant dπ​(G)=kπ​(G)/|G|πd_{\pi}(G)=k_{\pi}(G)/|G|_{\pi} seems to capture much information about the π\pi-structure of GG [19, 20, 46]. In particular, if π=p′\pi=p^{\prime} for some prime pp, then dp′​(G)d_{p^{\prime}}(G) captures information about the modular representations of GG over a field of characteristic pp [41]. Sangroniz characterized when dp′​(G)=dp′​(H)d_{p^{\prime}}(G)=d_{p^{\prime}}(H) representation-theoretically for HH a subgroup of a pp-solvable group GG in [40, Theorem 3.3].

    Now we define the class function Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} by

    Ππ,G​(g)={|𝐂G​(g)|if g∈G is a π-element0otherwise.\displaystyle\Pi_{\pi,G}(g)=\begin{cases}|\mathbf{C}_{G}(g)|&\text{if $g\in G$ is a $\pi$-element}\\ 0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

    We also define the scaled class function Δπ,G=Ππ,G/|G|π\Delta_{\pi,G}=\Pi_{\pi,G}/|G|_{\pi}. A straightforward calculation shows that [Ππ,G,1G]=kπ​(G)[\Pi_{\pi,G},1_{G}]=k_{\pi}(G) and [Δπ,G,1G]=dπ​(G)[\Delta_{\pi,G},1_{G}]=d_{\pi}(G).

    We also mention Robinson’s closely related generalized character defined by Ψ1,p,G​(g)=|𝐂G​(g)p|\Psi_{1,p,G}(g)=|\mathbf{C}_{G}(g)_{p}|, the number of pp-elements in 𝐂G​(g)\mathbf{C}_{G}(g), if g∈Gg\in G is pp-regular and 00 otherwise [39]. Robinson also defines a π\pi-variant in [39, Section 8].

    Example 2.7.

    (Local class functions.) The last example can also be put in a more general context. If X⊆GX\subseteq G is any subset closed under conjugation by GG, then we may define

    ΠX,G​(g)={|𝐂G​(g)|if g∈X0otherwise.\displaystyle\Pi_{X,G}(g)=\begin{cases}|\mathbf{C}_{G}(g)|&\text{if $g\in X$}\\ 0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

    Then [ΠX,G,1G][\Pi_{X,G},1_{G}] is simply the number of conjugacy classes in XX. If X=GπX=G_{\pi}, then we recover Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} from Example 2.6. If XX is the set of all real, resp. rational, elements of GG, then [ΠX,G,1G][\Pi_{X,G},1_{G}] is the number of real, resp. rational, classes. We will consider this class function in more detail in Section 4.

    To conclude this section, we consider a basis for the space of class functions consisting of characteristic functions, relaxing the condition that the basis vectors be normalized to 11: The collection of class functions xi^\widehat{x_{i}} for i=1,…,k⁡(G)i=1,\dots,k(G) defined by xi^​(g)=1\widehat{x_{i}}(g)=1 if g∈xiGg\in x_{i}^{G} and 00 otherwise is clearly a basis of cf⁡(G)\mathrm{cf}(G). It is an orthogonal but not orthonormal basis with respect to the usual inner product, however, since [xi^,xj^]=δi​j​|xiG|/|G|[\widehat{x_{i}},\widehat{x_{j}}]=\delta_{ij}|x_{i}^{G}|/|G|. Let 1^G\widehat{1}_{G} denote the characteristic function of the GG-conjugacy class consisting of the identity. Note that [1^G,1^G]=1/|G|[\widehat{1}_{G},\widehat{1}_{G}]=1/|G|. We now reformulate a result of Sangroniz in the language of class functions using this basis.

    Example 2.8.

    (pp-regular classes.) Consider the group invariant IG=kp′​(G)/|G|I_{G}=k_{p^{\prime}}(G)/|G|. Sangroniz characterized representation-theoretically when IG=IHI_{G}=I_{H} for H≤GH\leq G in [40, Theorem 2.1]. Now define the class function 𝐈G=kp′​(G)​1^G\mathbf{I}_{G}=k_{p^{\prime}}(G)\;\widehat{1}_{G} for a finite group GG, so that IG=[𝐈G,1^G]I_{G}=[\mathbf{I}_{G},\widehat{1}_{G}]. We can recast Sangroniz’ theorem in the following form using class functions:

    Theorem 2.9.

    [40, Theorem 2.1] Let H≤GH\leq G, and let pp be a prime. The following are equivalent:

    1. (i)

      𝐈G=(𝐈H)G\mathbf{I}_{G}=(\mathbf{I}_{H})^{G}.

    2. (ii)

      Restriction is a surjection IBrp​(G)→IBrp​(H)\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(G)\rightarrow\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(H) and [G:H][G:H] is not divisible by pp.

    Proof. (i) ⇒\Rightarrow (ii): If 𝐈G=(𝐈H)G\mathbf{I}_{G}=(\mathbf{I}_{H})^{G}, then kp′(G)=𝐈G(1)=(𝐈H)G(1)=[G:H]kp′(H)k_{p^{\prime}}(G)=\mathbf{I}_{G}(1)=(\mathbf{I}_{H})^{G}(1)=[G:H]k_{p^{\prime}}(H); that is, IG=IHI_{G}=I_{H}. By [40, Theorem 2.1], this means that [G:H][G:H] is not divisible by pp and every irreducible pp-Brauer character of GG restricts irreducibly to HH, so restriction defines a map IBrp​(G)→IBrp​(H)\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(G)\rightarrow\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(H). Since every irreducible Brauer character of HH lies under an irreducible Brauer character of GG by [37, Corollary 8.3], we have the desired surjection.

    (ii) ⇒\Rightarrow (i): Since all Brauer characters restrict irreducibly and p∤[G:H]p\nmid[G:H], we have 𝐈G(1)=kp′(G)=[G:H]kp′(H)=(𝐈H)G(1)\mathbf{I}_{G}(1)=k_{p^{\prime}}(G)=[G:H]k_{p^{\prime}}(H)=(\mathbf{I}_{H})^{G}(1) by [40, Theorem 2.1]. This completely characterizes the equality 𝐈G=(𝐈H)G\mathbf{I}_{G}=(\mathbf{I}_{H})^{G} since both sides vanish off the identity. ∎

    3. The local conjugating character

    In this section, we consider Questions (1) and (2) of the introduction for the “π\pi-local” conjugating character Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} and Δπ,G\Delta_{\pi,G} from Example 2.6. We consider Question (3) in the next section. Note that Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} interpolates between the character ΠG\Pi_{G} of the conjugating representation and the character ρG\rho_{G} of the regular representation: If GG is a π\pi-group then Ππ,G=ΠG\Pi_{\pi,G}=\Pi_{G}, while if GG is a π′\pi^{\prime}-group then Ππ,G=ρG\Pi_{\pi,G}=\rho_{G}.

    We now turn to Question (1) of the introduction. Note that the rational-valued class function Δπ,G\Delta_{\pi,G} is rarely a generalized character since [Δπ,G,1]=dπ​(G)[\Delta_{\pi,G},1]=d_{\pi}(G) and 0<dπ​(G)≤10<d_{\pi}(G)\leq 1 by [35, Lemma 3.5]. Our next theorem characterizes exactly when Δπ,G\Delta_{\pi,G} is a (generalized) character.

    Theorem 3.1.

    Let GG be a finite group, and let π\pi be a collection of primes. Then the following are equivalent:

    1. (i)

      Δπ,G\Delta_{\pi,G} is a character.

    2. (ii)

      Δπ,G\Delta_{\pi,G} is a generalized character.

    3. (iii)

      dπ​(G)=1d_{\pi}(G)=1.

    4. (iv)

      GG has a normal π\pi-complement and an abelian Hall π\pi-subgroup.

    Proof.

    The implication (i) ⇒\Rightarrow (ii) follows by definition. For (ii) ⇒\Rightarrow (iii), simply note that [Δπ,G,1G]∈ℤ[\Delta_{\pi,G},1_{G}]\in\mathbb{Z} and 0<dπ​(G)≤10<d_{\pi}(G)\leq 1 imply that dπ​(G)=1d_{\pi}(G)=1, which is (iii). We have (iii) ⇔\Leftrightarrow (iv) by [19, Proposition 7 b)]. Finally, consider (iv) ⇒\Rightarrow (i). We may write G=Hπ′⋊AπG=H_{\pi^{\prime}}\rtimes A_{\pi}, where Hπ′H_{\pi^{\prime}} is a normal Hall π′\pi^{\prime}-subgroup and AπA_{\pi} is an abelian Hall π\pi-subgroup. Since GG is π\pi-solvable, all Hall π\pi-subgroups of GG are conjugate and every π\pi-element is contained in a Hall π\pi-subgroup by a theorem of Hall. Hence, every π\pi-conjugacy class of GG has a representative in AπA_{\pi}. In fact, every element of AπA_{\pi} is the representative of a distinct π\pi-conjugacy class of GG: Otherwise, there exist distinct a,b∈Aπa,b\in A_{\pi} with a=bxa=b^{x} for some x∈Gx\in G. Write x=h​cx=hc with h∈Hπ′h\in H_{\pi^{\prime}} and c∈Aπc\in A_{\pi}. Since Hπ′​⊴​GH_{\pi^{\prime}}\trianglelefteq G, we have h′:=c−1​h​c∈Hπ′h^{\prime}:=c^{-1}hc\in H_{\pi^{\prime}}, and x=c​h′x=ch^{\prime}. As AπA_{\pi} is abelian, we have bc=bb^{c}=b, and so a=bx=bc​h′=bh′a=b^{x}=b^{ch^{\prime}}=b^{h^{\prime}}. But then b−1​a=[b,h′]∈Aπ∩Hπ′=1b^{-1}a=[b,h^{\prime}]\in A_{\pi}\cap H_{\pi^{\prime}}=1, and so a=ba=b, a contradiction. Now we calculate the multiplicity of the character χ∈Irr⁡(G)\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(G) in Δπ,G\Delta_{\pi,G} to be

    [Δπ,G,χ]\displaystyle[\Delta_{\pi,G},\chi] =1|G|​∑g∈Gπ|𝐂G​(g)|​χ⁡(g)¯|G|π=1|G|π​∑g∈Gπχ⁡(g)¯|gG|\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G_{\pi}}\frac{|\mathbf{C}_{G}(g)|\overline{\chi(g)}}{|G|_{\pi}}=\frac{1}{|G|_{\pi}}\sum_{g\in G_{\pi}}\frac{\overline{\chi(g)}}{|g^{G}|}
    =1|Aπ|​∑a∈Aπ|aG|​χ⁡(a)¯|aG|=1|Aπ|​∑a∈Aπχ⁡(a)¯=[1Aπ,χ|Aπ],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|A_{\pi}|}\sum_{a\in A_{\pi}}|a^{G}|\frac{\overline{\chi(a)}}{|a^{G}|}=\frac{1}{|A_{\pi}|}\sum_{a\in A_{\pi}}\overline{\chi(a)}=[1_{A_{\pi}},\chi|_{A_{\pi}}],

    which is a nonnegative integer since it is an inner product of characters of AπA_{\pi}. So Δπ,G\Delta_{\pi,G} is a character. ∎

    In contrast to Δπ,G\Delta_{\pi,G}, the class function Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} is always a generalized character.

    Theorem 3.2.

    Let GG be a finite group, and let π\pi be a collection of primes. Then Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} is a generalized character of GG.

    Proof.

    For every χ∈Irr⁡(G)\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(G), the multiplicity

    [Ππ,G,χ]=∑g∈Gπ|𝐂G​(g)|​χ⁡(g)¯|G|=∑g∈Gπχ⁡(g)¯|gG|=∑gG∈Clπ​(G)χ⁡(g)¯\displaystyle[\Pi_{\pi,G},\chi]=\sum_{g\in G_{\pi}}\frac{|\mathbf{C}_{G}(g)|\overline{\chi(g)}}{|G|}=\sum_{g\in G_{\pi}}\frac{\overline{\chi(g)}}{|g^{G}|}=\sum_{g^{G}\in\mathrm{Cl}_{\pi}(G)}\overline{\chi(g)}

    is an algebraic integer. Since the Galois group of the cyclotomic field ℚ|G|\mathbb{Q}_{|G|} permutes the conjugacy classes of GG (preserving the orders of elements), the multiplicity [Ππ,G,χ][\Pi_{\pi,G},\chi] is fixed by every such Galois automorphism, so it is rational. Hence, [Ππ,G,χ][\Pi_{\pi,G},\chi] is an integer and Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} is a generalized character. ∎

    Since the class function Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} is always a generalized character, it is then natural to ask when it is a character. In our next theorem, we show that Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} is always a character in some important special cases. These results were proved independently by Robinson in [39, Remark 5.1 and Theorem 8.1]; we prove the π=p′\pi=p^{\prime} case using different methods, but our proof of the π\pi-separable case is very similar, so we just sketch it.

    Theorem 3.3.

    Let π\pi be a collection of primes. If

    1. (i)

      π=p′\pi=p^{\prime} for some prime pp and GG is an arbitrary finite group or

    2. (ii)

      π\pi is arbitrary and GG is a π\pi-separable finite group,

    then Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} is a character of GG.

    Proof.

    (i) Let GG be an arbitrary finite group and π=p′\pi=p^{\prime} for some prime pp. For every χ∈Irr⁡(G)\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(G), define the decomposition numbers dχ,φd_{\chi,\varphi} by χ0=∑φ∈IBrp​(G)dχ,φ​φ\chi^{0}=\sum_{\varphi\in\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(G)}d_{\chi,\varphi}\varphi, where χ0\chi^{0} is the restriction of χ\chi to the pp-regular elements of GG. The decomposition numbers are nonnegative integers since χ0\chi^{0} is a Brauer character of GG by [37, Corollary 2.9]. Then for every φ∈IBrp​(G)\varphi\in\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(G) we may define the projective indecomposable character Φφ\Phi_{\varphi} associated to φ\varphi by Φφ=∑χ∈Irr⁡(G)dχ,φ​χ\Phi_{\varphi}=\sum_{\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(G)}d_{\chi,\varphi}\chi. Note that Φφ\Phi_{\varphi} is an ordinary character of GG since it is a nonnegative integral linear combination of characters of GG. Now, by [37, Theorem 2.13], the set {Φφ∣φ∈IBrp​(G)}\{\Phi_{\varphi}\mid\varphi\in\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(G)\} is a basis for those class functions of GG which vanish off of pp-regular elements. Since Πp′,G\Pi_{p^{\prime},G} vanishes off of pp-regular elements by definition, we have

    Πp′,G=∑φ∈IBrp​(G)eφ​Φφ\displaystyle\Pi_{p^{\prime},G}=\sum_{\varphi\in\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(G)}e_{\varphi}\Phi_{\varphi}

    for some eφ∈ℂe_{\varphi}\in\mathbb{C}. Now, it follows from [37, Theorem 2.13] that

    eφ¯=[φ,Πp′,G]0:=1|G|​∑g∈Gp′φ⁡(g)​Πp′,G​(g)¯.\displaystyle\overline{e_{\varphi}}=[\varphi,\Pi_{p^{\prime},G}]^{0}:=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G_{p^{\prime}}}\varphi(g)\overline{\Pi_{p^{\prime},G}(g)}.

    In addition, it follows from [37, Corollary 2.17] that eφ=eφ¯∈ℤe_{\varphi}=\overline{e_{\varphi}}\in\mathbb{Z} since Πp′,G\Pi_{p^{\prime},G} is a generalized character vanishing off of pp-regular elements by Theorem 3.2. (Indeed, [37, Corollary 2.17] shows that [φ,χ]0[\varphi,\chi]^{0} is an integer when χ\chi is any ordinary character vanishing off of pp-regular elements, and the same proof goes through for generalized characters vanishing off of pp-regular elements.)

    Thus, in order to prove that Πp′,G\Pi_{p^{\prime},G} is a character, it is enough to show that eφe_{\varphi} is nonnegative, since then Πp′,G\Pi_{p^{\prime},G} is a nonnegative integral sum of characters. Using the definition of Πp′,G\Pi_{p^{\prime},G}, we have

    eφ=1|G|​∑g∈Gp′|𝐂G​(g)|​φ​(g)=∑g∈Gp′φ⁡(g)|gG|=∑gG∈Clp′​(G)φ⁡(g).\displaystyle e_{\varphi}=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G_{p^{\prime}}}|\mathbf{C}_{G}(g)|\varphi(g)=\sum_{g\in G_{p^{\prime}}}\frac{\varphi(g)}{|g^{G}|}=\sum_{g^{G}\in\mathrm{Cl}_{p^{\prime}}(G)}\varphi(g).

    That is, eφe_{\varphi} is the sum of entries in the row of the Brauer character table corresponding to φ\varphi. Such sums have been investigated in [6, 7]. In particular, it is remarked in the proof of [6, Theorem 1.1] that [7, Example 1.8 and Proposition 2.2(b)] proves that the row sums in the Brauer character table are nonnegative real numbers. Hence, eφe_{\varphi} is a nonnegative integer and Πp′,G\Pi_{p^{\prime},G} is a character of GG.

    (ii) Now, if π\pi is an arbitrary collection of primes and GG is π\pi-separable, then an exactly analogous proof goes through. Namely, in place of the Brauer characters we have the so-called π\pi-partial characters, i.e. the restrictions of ordinary characters of GG to the π\pi-elements of GG. The collection Iπ​(G)I_{\pi}(G) of irreducible π\pi-partial characters consists of those π\pi-partial characters that cannot be written as a sum of two π\pi-partial characters. Then, in the same way as before, we may define decomposition numbers for each π\pi-partial character χ0\chi^{0} with χ∈Irr⁡(G)\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(G), which are necessarily nonnegative integers by the construction of π\pi-partial characters: The decomposition numbers simply reflect the decomposition of χ0\chi^{0} into the linearly independent irreducible π\pi-partial characters. Then, in the same way as before, we define projective indecomposable characters Φφ\Phi_{\varphi} for φ∈Iπ​(G)\varphi\in\mathrm{I}_{\pi}(G). It is proved in [24, Corollary 3.8] that the characters Φφ\Phi_{\varphi} constitute a basis for class functions vanishing off of π\pi-elements. Again, the multiplicity of Φφ\Phi_{\varphi} in Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} is an integer by [24, Problem 3.4] since Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} is a generalized character by Theorem 3.2; as before, the result is stated there for characters, but the same proof goes through for generalized characters. The multiplicity is equal to a row sum in the π\pi-partial character table of GG by [24, Problem 3.5]. It is remarked in the proof of [6, Theorem 2.4] that [7, Proposition 2.2(b)] proves that the row sums in the π\pi-partial character table are nonnegative real numbers. So the multiplicities must be nonnegative integers, and again Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} is a character of GG. ∎

    Remark 3.4.

    One can show that the row sums in the ordinary character table are nonnegative integers using the conjugating character [22, Problem 5.13]. In a nicely parallel result, the proof of Theorem 3.3 shows that the row sums in the pp-Brauer character table are nonnegative integers by using the “local” conjugating character Πp′,G\Pi_{p^{\prime},G}. This result sharpens [7, Proposition 2.2(b)], where it was shown that row sums in the pp-Brauer table are nonnegative real numbers.

    Supported by Theorem 3.3 and computational evidence, we state the following conjecture, which would answer a question of Robinson in [39, Section 8].

    Conjecture 3.5.

    Let GG be a finite group, and let π\pi be an arbitrary collection of primes. Then Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} is a character of GG; that is, [Ππ,G,χ]≥0[\Pi_{\pi,G},\chi]\geq 0 for all χ∈Irr⁡(G)\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(G).

    A counterexample to Conjecture 3.5 would consist of a finite group GG, a collection of primes π\pi and a character χ∈Irr⁡(G)\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(G) such that [Ππ,G,χ]<0[\Pi_{\pi,G},\chi]<0. A natural first place to look for such a counterexample is among those groups GG and characters χ∈Irr⁡(G)\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(G) whose multiplicities in the conjugating character ΠG\Pi_{G} are as small as possible, namely [ΠG,χ]=0[\Pi_{G},\chi]=0; the idea being that one could perhaps make a clever choice of π\pi to force the multiplicity [Ππ,G,χ][\Pi_{\pi,G},\chi] to be negative. If GG is a nonabelian simple group, the collection of such pairs (G,χ)(G,\chi) is remarkably small: [ΠG,χ]=0[\Pi_{G},\chi]=0 if and only if G≅PSUn​(q)G\cong\mathrm{PSU}_{n}(q) (n≥3n\geq 3) with nn coprime to 2​(q+1)2(q+1) and χ\chi is the Weil character of degree (qn−q)/(q+1)(q^{n}-q)/(q+1) [15, 16]. In our next theorem, we show that PSU3​(q)\mathrm{PSU}_{3}(q) with (3,q+1)=1(3,q+1)=1 and its Weil character χ\chi of degree q2−qq^{2}-q do not yield a counterexample to Conjecture 3.5 for any collection π\pi of primes.

    Note that Conjecture 3.5 is equivalent to the statement that for any finite group and any collection π\pi of primes, the partial row sum over π\pi-conjugacy classes in any row of the character table is a nonnegative integer, since for any χ∈Irr⁡(G)\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(G),

    [Ππ,G,χ]=∑g∈Gπ|𝐂G​(g)|​χ⁡(g)¯|G|=∑g∈Gπχ⁡(g)¯|gG|=∑gG∈Clπ​(G)χ⁡(g)¯=∑gG∈Clπ​(G)χ⁡(g),\displaystyle[\Pi_{\pi,G},\chi]=\sum_{g\in G_{\pi}}\frac{|\mathbf{C}_{G}(g)|\overline{\chi(g)}}{|G|}=\sum_{g\in G_{\pi}}\frac{\overline{\chi(g)}}{|g^{G}|}=\sum_{g^{G}\in\mathrm{Cl}_{\pi}(G)}\overline{\chi(g)}=\sum_{g^{G}\in\mathrm{Cl}_{\pi}(G)}\chi(g),

    where the last equality follows since Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} is a generalized character by Theorem 3.2. This is the statement that we prove in Theorem 3.6 for PSU3​(q)\mathrm{PSU}_{3}(q) and (3,q+1)=1(3,q+1)=1. We remark that this is not the approach taken in [15, 16] to investigate the multiplicities [ΠG,χ][\Pi_{G},\chi] for χ∈Irr⁡(G)\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(G), as the authors take advantage of the fact that ΠG\Pi_{G} decomposes into a sum of permutation characters on its conjugacy classes. (See [15, Lemma 2.1] for the consequences of this observation.) As we do not have such an interpretation of Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} – in particular, Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} is not the sum of permutation characters on π\pi-conjugacy classes, the latter being a character which takes the value |𝐂G​(g)π||\mathbf{C}_{G}(g)_{\pi}| on each element g∈Gg\in G – we consider the row sum of the character table directly.

    Theorem 3.6.

    If G≅PSU3​(q)G\cong\mathrm{PSU}_{3}(q) with (3,q+1)=1(3,q+1)=1 and χ\chi is the Weil character of degree q2−qq^{2}-q, then [Ππ,G,χ]≥0[\Pi_{\pi,G},\chi]\geq 0 for all collections π\pi of primes.

    Proof.

    To begin, we first calculate in GAP that [Ππ,G,χ]≥0[\Pi_{\pi,G},\chi]\geq 0 for all collections π\pi of primes and q=3,4,7,9q=3,4,7,9; these are the prime powers q≤9q\leq 9 with (3,q+1)=1(3,q+1)=1. So we may assume that q>9q>9. The character table of PSU3​(q)\mathrm{PSU}_{3}(q) is given in [42, Table 2], and the relevant information is summarized in Table 1. We omit information about classes on which χ\chi vanishes, as they will not contribute to the sum over conjugacy classes that calculates the multiplicity [Ππ,G,χ][\Pi_{\pi,G},\chi]. In Table 1, CiC_{i} labels the type of the conjugacy class as defined in [42, Table 2] whose elements are πi\pi_{i}-elements, NiN_{i} is the number of conjugacy classes of type CiC_{i}, and χ⁡(Ci)\chi(C_{i}) is the value of χ\chi at any element of CiC_{i}. Note that elements in distinct members of the family of classes CiC_{i} need not have the same order, but just the same character value.

    Assume for contradiction that there is some qq and collection π\pi of primes such that [Ππ,G,χ]<0[\Pi_{\pi,G},\chi]<0; that is, the sum over π\pi-conjugacy classes in the row of the character table corresponding to χ\chi is negative. Any collection π\pi admits the contribution from N1​χ​(C1)=q2−qN_{1}\chi(C_{1})=q^{2}-q. Now we use the character table to consider which primes are forced to belong to such a π\pi.

    We first show that π⁡(q+1)⊆π\pi(q+1)\subseteq\pi. The only negative contributions come from class types C2C_{2}, C4C_{4} and C8C_{8}. Note that we must include some classes of type C4C_{4} because N1​χ​(C1)+N2​χ​(C2)+N8​χ​(C8)=23​q2−53​qN_{1}\chi(C_{1})+N_{2}\chi(C_{2})+N_{8}\chi(C_{8})=\frac{2}{3}q^{2}-\frac{5}{3}q, which is greater than zero as q>2q>2. Since χ⁡(C4)=−(q−1)\chi(C_{4})=-(q-1), the number of classes of type C4C_{4} that we must include to obtain a negative multiplicity is bounded below by

    23​q2−53​qq−1=23​q−qq−1>12​(q+1)for ​q>9.\displaystyle\frac{\frac{2}{3}q^{2}-\frac{5}{3}q}{q-1}=\frac{2}{3}q-\frac{q}{q-1}>\frac{1}{2}(q+1)\qquad\text{for }q>9.

    By [42, Table 2], each class of type C4C_{4} has a representative in a cyclic subgroup TT of order q+1q+1, namely T={diag⁡(a,a,a−2)∣aq+1=1}T=\{\mathrm{diag}(a,a,a^{-2})\mid a^{q+1}=1\}, contained in a maximal torus of order (q+1)2(q+1)^{2}, and distinct nonidentity elements of TT lie in distinct classes. Therefore, given any subset τ⊆π⁡(q+1)\tau\subseteq\pi(q+1) that we choose to include in our π\pi, the identity and the representatives that we obtain in a class of type C4C_{4} constitute a maximal cyclic τ\tau-subgroup of TT. The above calculation shows that we must include more than half the elements of TT. So by Lagrange’s theorem, all the elements of TT must be included. This means all of π⁡(q+1)\pi(q+1) is included in π\pi, which is what we wanted to show.

    Therefore, [Ππ,G,χ][\Pi_{\pi,G},\chi] includes the contribution N4​χ​(C4)=−(q2−q)N_{4}\chi(C_{4})=-(q^{2}-q). But since π6=π⁡(q+1)\pi_{6}=\pi(q+1) as well, we also have the contribution N6​χ​(C6)=+13​(q2−q)N_{6}\chi(C_{6})=+\frac{1}{3}(q^{2}-q). So if π=π⁡(q+1)\pi=\pi(q+1), we have [Ππ,G,χ]=13​(q2−q)[\Pi_{\pi,G},\chi]=\frac{1}{3}(q^{2}-q), and we need to add more primes if we are to obtain a negative multiplicity.

    Next, notice that if we add the defining prime π⁡(q)\pi(q) to π\pi, then since π⁡(q+1)⊆π\pi(q+1)\subseteq\pi, we obtain the contributions from classes of types C2C_{2} and C5C_{5}, which exactly cancel. Therefore, it is inconsequential whether we include π⁡(q)\pi(q) in π\pi or not, as in both cases we are left with [Ππ,G,χ]=13​(q2−q)[\Pi_{\pi,G},\chi]=\frac{1}{3}(q^{2}-q) at this point.

    Our last remaining choice is whether to add some subset of π⁡(q2−q+1)\pi(q^{2}-q+1) to π\pi. The contribution from all classes of type C8C_{8} is N8​χ​(C8)=−13​(q2−q)N_{8}\chi(C_{8})=-\frac{1}{3}(q^{2}-q), so regardless of which remaining primes we add to π\pi, we always have [Ππ,G,χ]≥0[\Pi_{\pi,G},\chi]\geq 0. This contradiction concludes the proof. ∎

    Having addressed the issue of Δπ,G\Delta_{\pi,G} and Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} being (generalized) characters, we now turn to the decomposition of Δπ,G\Delta_{\pi,G} and Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G}. This is Question (2) of the introduction. It is natural to first ask when Δπ,G\Delta_{\pi,G} or Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} is an irreducible character. That is, when are all but one of the multiplicities zero? The next theorem shows that this only identifies some degenerate cases.

    Theorem 3.7.

    Let GG be a finite group and let π\pi be a collection of primes. Then Δπ,G\Delta_{\pi,G} is an irreducible character of GG if and only if GG is an abelian π\pi-group. The generalized character Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} is an irreducible character of GG if and only if GG is the trivial group.

    Proof.

    Assume that Δπ,G\Delta_{\pi,G} or Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} is irreducible. The key here is to simply recall that [Δπ,G,1G]=dπ​(G)>0[\Delta_{\pi,G},1_{G}]=d_{\pi}(G)>0 and [Ππ,G,1G]=kπ​(G)>0[\Pi_{\pi,G},1_{G}]=k_{\pi}(G)>0. So Δπ,G\Delta_{\pi,G} or Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} is irreducible if and only if it is equal to the trivial character. In particular, Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} cannot vanish on any element of GG in either case, so GG is a π\pi-group by the definition of Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G}. Now, we have Δπ,G=1G\Delta_{\pi,G}=1_{G}, so 1=[Δπ,G,1G]=dπ​(G)=d⁡(G)1=[\Delta_{\pi,G},1_{G}]=d_{\pi}(G)=d(G), so GG is an abelian π\pi-group. Similarly, Ππ,G=1G\Pi_{\pi,G}=1_{G}, so 1=[Ππ,G,1G]=kπ​(G)=k⁡(G)1=[\Pi_{\pi,G},1_{G}]=k_{\pi}(G)=k(G), so GG has only one conjugacy class, i.e. GG is the trivial group.

    The reverse implications are obvious because Δπ,G=1G\Delta_{\pi,G}=1_{G} and Ππ,G=1G\Pi_{\pi,G}=1_{G} under the assumptions of the theorem. ∎

    Theorem 3.7 shows that Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} has only one constituent if and only if GG is the trivial group. We might then suspect that Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} has many constituents when GG is nontrivial. As we mentioned above, this is a well-known and much-studied property of the conjugating character ΠG\Pi_{G}. Decomposing Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} into its constituents seems difficult in general, but it could be interesting to study its decomposition for some particular classes of groups and values of π\pi. For example, it is known that [Π2′,Sn,χ]>0[\Pi_{2^{\prime},S_{n}},\chi]>0 for all χ∈Irr⁡(Sn)\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(S_{n}) and n≥1n\geq 1 [43, Theorem 4.9]; this is more than what is implied by Theorem 3.3(i) with p=2p=2.

    4. Characterizing group structure

    In this section, we turn to Question (3) of the introduction, which asks to characterize group structure in terms of the behavior of a class function. We can state our first result for the more general class functions of Example 2.7. Recall that if X⊆GX\subseteq G is any subset closed under conjugation, then we define ΠX,G​(g)=|𝐂G​(g)|\Pi_{X,G}(g)=|\mathbf{C}_{G}(g)| if g∈Xg\in X and 00 otherwise. We write ClX​(G)\mathrm{Cl}_{X}(G) to denote the set of GG-conjugacy classes contained in XX. Letting X=GπX=G_{\pi}, the set of π\pi-elements of GG, recovers Ππ,G\Pi_{\pi,G} from the last section.

    Theorem 4.1.

    Let HH be a subgroup of a finite group GG. Let X⊆HX\subseteq H be a subset closed under conjugation by HH, and let Y⊆GY\subseteq G be a subset closed under conjugation by GG. The following are equivalent:

    1. (i)

      (ΠX,H)G=ΠY,G(\Pi_{X,H})^{G}=\Pi_{Y,G}.

    2. (ii)

      The map hH↦hGh^{H}\mapsto h^{G} is a bijection ClX​(H)→ClY​(G)\mathrm{Cl}_{X}(H)\rightarrow\mathrm{Cl}_{Y}(G).

    Proof.

    Letting g∈Gg\in G, we begin by deriving a formula for (ΠX,H)G​(g)(\Pi_{X,H})^{G}(g). The set gG∩Xg^{G}\cap X is fixed setwise under conjugation by elements of HH, so it is equal to a (possibly empty) union h1H∪⋯∪hmHh_{1}^{H}\cup\cdots\cup h_{m}^{H} of HH-conjugacy classes in XX. If gG∩Xg^{G}\cap X is nonempty, then using the definition of an induced character (see, in particular, [22, p. 64]), we have that

    (ΠX,H)G​(g)=|𝐂G​(g)|​∑i=1mΠX,H​(hi)|𝐂H​(hi)|=m​|𝐂G​(g)|.\displaystyle(\Pi_{X,H})^{G}(g)=|\mathbf{C}_{G}(g)|\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{\Pi_{X,H}(h_{i})}{|\mathbf{C}_{H}(h_{i})|}=m|\mathbf{C}_{G}(g)|.

    We write this as

    (∗*) (ΠX,H)G​(g)={m​|𝐂G​(g)|if ​gG∩X​ is a union of m≥1 H-classes,0if ​gG∩X=∅.\displaystyle(\Pi_{X,H})^{G}(g)=\begin{cases}m|\mathbf{C}_{G}(g)|&\text{if }g^{G}\cap X\text{ is a union of $m\geq 1$ $H$-classes,}\\ 0&\text{if }g^{G}\cap X=\emptyset.\end{cases}

    Now we continue with the proof of the theorem.

    (ii) ⇒\Rightarrow (i): First note that X⊆YX\subseteq Y since, if h∈Xh\in X, then hG∈ClY​(G)h^{G}\in\mathrm{Cl}_{Y}(G) by assumption, and so h∈Yh\in Y. Now let g∈Gg\in G. If g∉Yg\not\in Y, then ΠY,G​(g)=0\Pi_{Y,G}(g)=0 by definition. Since X⊆YX\subseteq Y, gG∩X⊆gG∩Y=∅g^{G}\cap X\subseteq g^{G}\cap Y=\emptyset, and so (ΠX,H)G​(g)=0(\Pi_{X,H})^{G}(g)=0 as well by Equation ( ∗ ‣ 4). Now assume that g∈Yg\in Y. By the bijection in (ii), gG∩Xg^{G}\cap X is exactly one HH-class: surjectivity gives some h∈Hh\in H with h∈gG∩Xh\in g^{G}\cap X, and if two distinct HH-classes sat inside gG∩Xg^{G}\cap X, they would have the same image, contradicting injectivity. Therefore, m=1m=1 in ( ∗ ‣ 4), and so (ΠX,H)G​(g)=|𝐂G​(g)|=ΠY,G​(g)(\Pi_{X,H})^{G}(g)=|\mathbf{C}_{G}(g)|=\Pi_{Y,G}(g).

    (i) ⇒\Rightarrow (ii): Let h∈Xh\in X. Then of course hG∩X≠∅h^{G}\cap X\neq\emptyset, and so (ΠX,H)G​(h)≠0(\Pi_{X,H})^{G}(h)\neq 0 by ( ∗ ‣ 4). Since (ΠX,H)G​(h)=ΠY,G​(h)(\Pi_{X,H})^{G}(h)=\Pi_{Y,G}(h), this means, in particular, that h∈Yh\in Y. So again X⊆YX\subseteq Y. Therefore, hH↦hGh^{H}\mapsto h^{G} is indeed a map ClX​(H)→ClY​(G)\mathrm{Cl}_{X}(H)\rightarrow\mathrm{Cl}_{Y}(G).

    The map is injective: Let h1H,h2H∈ClX​(H)h_{1}^{H},h_{2}^{H}\in\mathrm{Cl}_{X}(H) such that h1G=h2G∈ClY​(G)h_{1}^{G}=h_{2}^{G}\in\mathrm{Cl}_{Y}(G). By assumption, (ΠX,H)G​(h1)=ΠY,G​(h1)(\Pi_{X,H})^{G}(h_{1})=\Pi_{Y,G}(h_{1}), which means that h1G∩Xh_{1}^{G}\cap X is a single HH-class, namely h1Hh_{1}^{H}, by ( ∗ ‣ 4). In the same way, h2G∩X=h2Hh_{2}^{G}\cap X=h_{2}^{H}. Therefore, h1H=h1G∩X=h2G∩X=h2Hh_{1}^{H}=h_{1}^{G}\cap X=h_{2}^{G}\cap X=h_{2}^{H}.

    The map is surjective: Let gG∈ClY​(G)g^{G}\in\mathrm{Cl}_{Y}(G). By assumption, (ΠX,H)G​(g)=ΠY,G​(g)(\Pi_{X,H})^{G}(g)=\Pi_{Y,G}(g), which means that gG∩Xg^{G}\cap X is exactly one HH-class lying in XX, say hH∈ClX​(H)h^{H}\in\mathrm{Cl}_{X}(H), by ( ∗ ‣ 4). Hence, hH↦hG=gGh^{H}\mapsto h^{G}=g^{G}. ∎

    We note that in all of our applications of Theorem 4.1, X=Y∩HX=Y\cap H.

    Theorem 4.1 characterizes when (ΠX,H)G=ΠY,G(\Pi_{X,H})^{G}=\Pi_{Y,G} group-theoretically. We are also interested in a representation-theoretic characterization of such equalities. As our starting point, consider the following restatement of a theorem of Sangroniz.

    Theorem 4.2.

    [40, Theorem 3.3] Let pp be a prime, and let HH be a subgroup of a finite pp-solvable group GG. Then the following are equivalent:

    1. (i)

      dp′​(G)=dp′​(H)d_{p^{\prime}}(G)=d_{p^{\prime}}(H).

    2. (ii)

      Restriction is a surjection IBrp​(G)→IBrp​(H)\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(G)\rightarrow\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(H).

    Proof.

    Taking π=p′\pi=p^{\prime} in [40, Theorem 3.3] for the pp-solvable group GG, dp′​(G)=dp′​(H)d_{p^{\prime}}(G)=d_{p^{\prime}}(H) if and only if all irreducible Brauer characters of GG restrict irreducibly to HH. Since every irreducible Brauer character of HH is a constituent of the restriction of some irreducible Brauer character of GG by [37, Corollary 8.3], this is equivalent to restriction being a surjection IBrp​(G)→IBrp​(H)\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(G)\rightarrow\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(H). ∎

    Since (Δp′,H)G=Δp′,G(\Delta_{p^{\prime},H})^{G}=\Delta_{p^{\prime},G} implies that dp′​(H)=dp′​(G)d_{p^{\prime}}(H)=d_{p^{\prime}}(G) by Frobenius reciprocity, the representation-theoretic characterization of (Δp′,H)G=Δp′,G(\Delta_{p^{\prime},H})^{G}=\Delta_{p^{\prime},G} in the next theorem is a refinement of Theorem 4.2. We show that it is a strict refinement in Example 4.4.

    Theorem 4.3.

    Let pp be a prime, and let HH be a subgroup of a finite group GG.

    (1) If restriction is a bijection IBrp​(G)→IBrp​(H)\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(G)\rightarrow\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(H), then (Πp′,H)G=Πp′,G(\Pi_{p^{\prime},H})^{G}=\Pi_{p^{\prime},G}, but the converse does not hold.

    (2) Now assume that GG is pp-solvable. Then the following are equivalent:

    1. (i)

      (Δp′,H)G=Δp′,G(\Delta_{p^{\prime},H})^{G}=\Delta_{p^{\prime},G}.

    2. (ii)

      Restriction is a bijection IBrp​(G)→IBrp​(H)\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(G)\rightarrow\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(H) and [G:H]p′=1[G:H]_{p^{\prime}}=1.

    In particular, either condition in (2) implies that (Πp′,H)G=Πp′,G(\Pi_{p^{\prime},H})^{G}=\Pi_{p^{\prime},G}.

    Proof.

    (1) We first show that if restriction is a bijection IBrp​(G)→IBrp​(H)\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(G)\rightarrow\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(H), then hH↦hGh^{H}\mapsto h^{G} is a bijection Clp′​(H)→Clp′​(G)\mathrm{Cl}_{p^{\prime}}(H)\rightarrow\mathrm{Cl}_{p^{\prime}}(G). This shows that (Πp′,H)G=Πp′,G(\Pi_{p^{\prime},H})^{G}=\Pi_{p^{\prime},G} by Theorem 4.1. It is clearly a well-defined map. Since |IBrp​(G)|=|Clp′​(G)||\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(G)|=|\mathrm{Cl}_{p^{\prime}}(G)|, the bijection implies that |Clp′​(G)|=|Clp′​(H)||\mathrm{Cl}_{p^{\prime}}(G)|=|\mathrm{Cl}_{p^{\prime}}(H)|. So we need only show that hH↦hGh^{H}\mapsto h^{G} is an injective map Clp′​(H)→Clp′​(G)\mathrm{Cl}_{p^{\prime}}(H)\rightarrow\mathrm{Cl}_{p^{\prime}}(G); that is, hG∩Hh^{G}\cap H is at most one HH-class. If not, there exists some irreducible Brauer character ψ∈IBrp​(H)\psi\in\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(H) that takes different values on the distinct HH-classes h1H,h2H⊆hG∩Hh_{1}^{H},h_{2}^{H}\subseteq h^{G}\cap H since IBrp​(H)\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(H) spans the vector space of complex-valued class functions on Hp′H_{p^{\prime}}. That is, ψ⁡(h1)≠ψ⁡(h2)\psi(h_{1})\neq\psi(h_{2}). Since restriction IBrp​(G)→IBrp​(H)\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(G)\rightarrow\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(H) is a bijection, ψ=φH\psi=\varphi_{H} for some φ∈IBrp​(G)\varphi\in\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(G). But φ\varphi is a class function on GG, so ψ⁡(h1)=φH​(h1)=φH​(h2)=ψ⁡(h2)\psi(h_{1})=\varphi_{H}(h_{1})=\varphi_{H}(h_{2})=\psi(h_{2}), a contradiction.

    To show that the converse fails, consider the following example identified by Navarro [38]. Let GG be the solvable Frobenius group (C3×C3)⋊C8(C_{3}\times C_{3})\rtimes C_{8} of order 7272 with C8C_{8} permuting the 88 elements of order 33 in C3×C3C_{3}\times C_{3}; this is SmallGroup(72,39) in GAP. Let H≤GH\leq G be isomorphic to S3\mathrm{S}_{3}, and let p=2p=2. Then [G:H]p′=3[G:H]_{p^{\prime}}=3. Both GG and HH have just one nonidentity class of 22-regular elements, so hH↦hGh^{H}\mapsto h^{G} is a bijection Cl2′​(H)→Cl2′​(G)\mathrm{Cl}_{2^{\prime}}(H)\rightarrow\mathrm{Cl}_{2^{\prime}}(G). This means (Π2′,H)G=Π2′,G(\Pi_{2^{\prime},H})^{G}=\Pi_{2^{\prime},G} by Theorem 4.1. However, the only nonlinear degree of an irreducible 22-Brauer character of GG is 88, and that of HH is 22; so restriction is not even a map IBr2​(G)→IBr2​(H)\mathrm{IBr}_{2}(G)\rightarrow\mathrm{IBr}_{2}(H), let alone a bijection.

    (2) First note that since Δp′,G=(1/|G|p′)​Πp′,G\Delta_{p^{\prime},G}=(1/|G|_{p^{\prime}})\Pi_{p^{\prime},G} by definition, Equation ( ∗ ‣ 4) in the proof of Theorem 4.1 implies that

    (Δp′,H)G​(g)={m​|𝐂G​(g)||H|p′if gG∩Hp′ is a union of m≥1 H-classes0if gG∩Hp′=∅\displaystyle(\Delta_{p^{\prime},H})^{G}(g)=\begin{cases}m\dfrac{|\mathbf{C}_{G}(g)|}{|H|_{p^{\prime}}}&\text{if $g^{G}\cap H_{p^{\prime}}$ is a union of $m\geq 1$ $H$-classes}\\ 0&\text{if $g^{G}\cap H_{p^{\prime}}=\emptyset$}\end{cases}

    for all g∈Gg\in G. Note that we have taken Y=Gp′Y=G_{p^{\prime}} and X=Y∩H=Hp′X=Y\cap H=H_{p^{\prime}} in Theorem 4.1. In particular, we have (Δp′,H)G=Δp′,G(\Delta_{p^{\prime},H})^{G}=\Delta_{p^{\prime},G} if and only if for every pp-regular g∈Gg\in G

    |𝐂G​(g)||G|p′=Δp′,G​(g)=(Δp′,H)G​(g)=m​|𝐂G​(g)||H|p′\displaystyle\frac{|\mathbf{C}_{G}(g)|}{|G|_{p^{\prime}}}=\Delta_{p^{\prime},G}(g)=(\Delta_{p^{\prime},H})^{G}(g)=m\frac{|\mathbf{C}_{G}(g)|}{|H|_{p^{\prime}}}

    and (Δp′,H)G​(g)=0=Δp′,G​(g)(\Delta_{p^{\prime},H})^{G}(g)=0=\Delta_{p^{\prime},G}(g) for all pp-singular g∈Gg\in G. Summarizing the situation implied by this equation, we have

    (Δp′,H)G=Δp′,G\displaystyle(\Delta_{p^{\prime},H})^{G}=\Delta_{p^{\prime},G}
    ⇔[G:H]p′=1 and m=1 for every gG∈Clp′​(G)\displaystyle\iff\text{$[G:H]_{p^{\prime}}=1$ and $m=1$ for every $g^{G}\in\mathrm{Cl}_{p^{\prime}}(G)$}
    ⇔[G:H]p′=1 and (Πp′,H)G=Πp′,G.\displaystyle\iff[G:H]_{p^{\prime}}=1\text{ and }(\Pi_{p^{\prime},H})^{G}=\Pi_{p^{\prime},G}.

    (i) ⇒\Rightarrow (ii): As we have mentioned before, (Δp′,H)G=Δp′,G(\Delta_{p^{\prime},H})^{G}=\Delta_{p^{\prime},G} implies that dp′​(H)=dp′​(G)d_{p^{\prime}}(H)=d_{p^{\prime}}(G). So restriction is a surjection IBrp​(G)→IBrp​(H)\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(G)\rightarrow\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(H) by Theorem 4.2. By what we just showed, (i) implies that [G:H]p′=1[G:H]_{p^{\prime}}=1 and (Πp′,H)G=Πp′,G(\Pi_{p^{\prime},H})^{G}=\Pi_{p^{\prime},G}. Therefore, |IBrp​(H)|=|Clp′​(H)|=|Clp′​(G)|=|IBrp​(G)||\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(H)|=|\mathrm{Cl}_{p^{\prime}}(H)|=|\mathrm{Cl}_{p^{\prime}}(G)|=|\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(G)| by Theorem 4.1, and so restriction is a bijection.

    (ii) ⇒\Rightarrow (i): By (1), (Πp′,H)G=Πp′,G(\Pi_{p^{\prime},H})^{G}=\Pi_{p^{\prime},G}, and the additional assumption that [G:H]p′=1[G:H]_{p^{\prime}}=1 ensures that (Δp′,H)G=Δp′,G(\Delta_{p^{\prime},H})^{G}=\Delta_{p^{\prime},G} by what we just showed. ∎

    Theorem 4.2 cannot be extended in either direction when GG is not pp-solvable; see the examples due to G. Navarro at the end of [41]. So of course our Theorem 4.3(2) cannot be extended to non-pp-solvable groups. The next example shows that Theorem 4.3(2) is a strict refinement of Theorem 4.2.

    Example 4.4.

    We show that there exists a pp-solvable group GG and subgroup H≤GH\leq G such that dp′​(G)=dp′​(H)d_{p^{\prime}}(G)=d_{p^{\prime}}(H) but Δp′,G≠(Δp′,H)G\Delta_{p^{\prime},G}\neq(\Delta_{p^{\prime},H})^{G}; that is, the invariant dp′​(G)d_{p^{\prime}}(G) cannot distinguish between GG and HH, but Δp′,G\Delta_{p^{\prime},G} can. So Δp′,G\Delta_{p^{\prime},G} accomplishes the task of distinguishing groups by their “timbre” as set out in the introduction.

    In fact, if GG is pp-solvable and the invariants are equal, then the class functions are equal if and only if [G:H]p′=1[G:H]_{p^{\prime}}=1: The forward direction follows directly from Theorem 4.3(2). For the reverse direction, dp′​(G)=dp′​(H)d_{p^{\prime}}(G)=d_{p^{\prime}}(H) implies restriction is a surjection by Theorem 4.2, and [G:H]p′=1[G:H]_{p^{\prime}}=1 implies furthermore that kp′​(G)=kp′​(H)k_{p^{\prime}}(G)=k_{p^{\prime}}(H). So restriction is a bijection, and we may apply Theorem 4.3(2).

    Let G=S4G=\mathrm{S}_{4}, H=A4H=\mathrm{A}_{4} and p=3p=3. The group GG is solvable, and so it is 33-solvable. Then d3′​(G)=1/2=d3′​(H)d_{3^{\prime}}(G)=1/2=d_{3^{\prime}}(H), but [G:H]3′=2>1[G:H]_{3^{\prime}}=2>1, so (Δ3′,H)G≠Δ3′,G(\Delta_{3^{\prime},H})^{G}\neq\Delta_{3^{\prime},G} by Theorem 4.3(2). More explicitly, they differ at the identity element, for example: Δ3′,G​(1)=|G|/|G|3′=3\Delta_{3^{\prime},G}(1)=|G|/|G|_{3^{\prime}}=3 and (Δ3′,H)G(1)=[G:H]⋅|H|/|H|3′=6(\Delta_{3^{\prime},H})^{G}(1)=[G:H]\cdot|H|/|H|_{3^{\prime}}=6. Regarding the different “timbres” of GG and HH, we have for the sign character ϵ∈Irr⁡(S4)\epsilon\in\mathrm{Irr}(\mathrm{S}_{4}) that

    [Δ3′,G,ϵ]=18​(ϵ⁡(1)+ϵ⁡((12)​(34))+ϵ⁡((12))+ϵ⁡((1234)))=18​(1+1−1−1)=0,\displaystyle[\Delta_{3^{\prime},G},\epsilon]=\frac{1}{8}(\epsilon(1)+\epsilon((12)(34))+\epsilon((12))+\epsilon((1234)))=\frac{1}{8}(1+1-1-1)=0,

    where we recall that the multiplicity [Π3′,G,ϵ][\Pi_{3^{\prime},G},\epsilon] is simply the sum over the 33-regular classes of GG in the row of the character table corresponding to ϵ\epsilon and Δ3′,G=(1/|G|3′)​Π3′,G\Delta_{3^{\prime},G}=(1/|G|_{3^{\prime}})\Pi_{3^{\prime},G}. On the other hand,

    [(Δ3′,H)G,ϵ]=[Δ3′,H,ϵ|H]=[Δ3′,H,1H]=d3′​(H)=12.\displaystyle[(\Delta_{3^{\prime},H})^{G},\epsilon]=[\Delta_{3^{\prime},H},\epsilon|_{H}]=[\Delta_{3^{\prime},H},1_{H}]=d_{3^{\prime}}(H)=\frac{1}{2}.

    So the “fundamental frequency” (i.e. the multiplicity of 1G1_{G}) does not distinguish GG and HH, but a “higher harmonic” (i.e. the multiplicity of ϵ\epsilon) does distinguish them.

    It is important to note that Theorem 4.3 is vacuous if GG is a p′p^{\prime}-group:

    Theorem 4.5.

    Let pp be a prime, and let HH be a subgroup of an arbitrary finite group GG. Suppose that |G||G| is not divisible by pp. Then any of the following statements imply that G=HG=H:

    1. (i)

      (Δp′,H)G=Δp′,G(\Delta_{p^{\prime},H})^{G}=\Delta_{p^{\prime},G}.

    2. (ii)

      (Πp′,H)G=Πp′,G(\Pi_{p^{\prime},H})^{G}=\Pi_{p^{\prime},G}.

    3. (iii)

      The map hH↦hGh^{H}\mapsto h^{G} is a bijection Clp′​(H)→Clp′​(G)\mathrm{Cl}_{p^{\prime}}(H)\rightarrow\mathrm{Cl}_{p^{\prime}}(G).

    4. (iv)

      Restriction is a bijection IBrp​(G)→IBrp​(H)\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(G)\rightarrow\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(H).

    Proof.

    If (i) holds, then 1=[G:H]p′=[G:H]1=[G:H]_{p^{\prime}}=[G:H] by Theorem 4.3(2) since GG is pp-solvable. Now assume (iii), which is equivalent to (ii) by Theorem 4.1. Let g∈Gg\in G be an arbitrary element, and assume for contradiction that H<GH<G. Since Clp′​(G)=Cl​(G)\mathrm{Cl}_{p^{\prime}}(G)=\mathrm{Cl}(G), gG∩Hg^{G}\cap H is nonempty by assumption. Hence, gg is contained in some GG-conjugate of HH. But then GG is covered by the conjugates of a proper subgroup, a contradiction. Finally, assume (iv). Then IBrp​(G)=Irr​(G)\mathrm{IBr}_{p}(G)=\mathrm{Irr}(G) by [37, Theorem 2.12], and the bijection implies that |G|=∑χ∈Irr⁡(G)χH​(1)2=|H||G|=\sum_{\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(G)}\chi_{H}(1)^{2}=|H|. ∎

    To conclude this section, we show that the class function ΠX,G\Pi_{X,G} is always a character when XX is the collection of real elements of GG; that is, XX consists of all elements of GG that are conjugate to their inverse.

    Theorem 4.6.

    Let GG be an arbitrary finite group, and let R⊆GR\subseteq G be the collection of real elements of GG. Then ΠR,G\Pi_{R,G} is a character of GG.

    Proof.

    Recall that the second orthogonality relation [22, Theorem 2.18] applied to the elements g,g−1∈Gg,g^{-1}\in G states that

    ∑χ∈Irr⁡(G)χ⁡(g)​χ⁡(g−1)¯={|𝐂G​(g)|if g is conjugate to g−10otherwise.=ΠR,G​(g).\displaystyle\sum_{\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(G)}\chi(g)\overline{\chi(g^{-1})}=\begin{cases}|\mathbf{C}_{G}(g)|&\text{if $g$ is conjugate to $g^{-1}$}\\ 0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\;=\;\Pi_{R,G}(g).

    Therefore, ΠR,G​(g)=∑χ∈Irr⁡(G)χ2​(g)\Pi_{R,G}(g)=\sum_{\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(G)}\chi^{2}(g). Since products of characters are characters (see [22, Corollary 4.2]), ΠR,G\Pi_{R,G} is also a character. ∎

    5. A dual construction

    Up to now, we have extended a group invariant IGI_{G} to a class function 𝐈G\mathbf{I}_{G} by encoding the original invariant IGI_{G} in the sum of values normalized by |G||G|; that is, (1/|G|)​∑g∈G𝐈G​(g)=[𝐈G,1G]=IG(1/|G|)\sum_{g\in G}\mathbf{I}_{G}(g)=[\mathbf{I}_{G},1_{G}]=I_{G}. We now consider a dual construction in which an invariant IGI_{G} is encoded in a class function 𝐈G\mathbf{I}_{G} as the sum of multiplicities of the irreducible characters normalized by |G||G|, namely IG=(1/|G|)​∑χ∈Irr⁡(G)[𝐈G,χ]I_{G}=(1/|G|)\sum_{\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(G)}[\mathbf{I}_{G},\chi]. We consider one interesting example of this dual construction. For a prime pp, define the class function (character) 𝐃p′​(G)=∑p∤χ⁡(1)χ\mathbf{D}_{p^{\prime}}(G)=\sum_{p\nmid\chi(1)}\chi, where the sum is taken over all irreducible characters of a finite group GG whose degree is not divisible by pp. This gives rise to an invariant

    Dp′​(G)=1|G|​∑χ∈Irr⁡(G)[𝐃p′​(G),χ]=|Irrp′​(G)||G|.\displaystyle D_{p^{\prime}}(G)=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(G)}[\mathbf{D}_{p^{\prime}}(G),\chi]=\frac{|\mathrm{Irr}_{p^{\prime}}(G)|}{|G|}.

    We first prove a bound for Dp′​(G)D_{p^{\prime}}(G). In the proof, we use the recently-proved McKay Conjecture [5].

    Theorem 5.1.

    Let GG be a finite group, let pp be a prime, and let PP be a Sylow pp-subgroup of GG. By Schur–Zassenhaus, we may write a Sylow pp-normalizer as 𝐍G​(P)=P⋊H\mathbf{N}_{G}(P)=P\rtimes H. We have

    Dp′(G)≤1|P′|×1[H:𝐂H(P/P′)].\displaystyle D_{p^{\prime}}(G)\leq\frac{1}{|P^{\prime}|}\times\frac{1}{[H:\mathbf{C}_{H}(P/P^{\prime})]}.
    Proof.

    Denote the quantity on the right-hand side of the inequality in the statement of the theorem by b⁡(G)b(G). Suppose for contradiction that the theorem is false. Let GG be a counterexample of minimal order, so b​(G)<Dp′​(G)b(G)<D_{p^{\prime}}(G). We have |Irrp′​(G)|=|Irrp′​(𝐍G​(P))||\mathrm{Irr}_{p^{\prime}}(G)|=|\mathrm{Irr}_{p^{\prime}}(\mathbf{N}_{G}(P))| by the McKay Conjecture, so

    b⁡(G)<|Irrp′​(G)||G|=|Irrp′​(𝐍G​(P))||G|≤|Irrp′​(𝐍G​(P))||𝐍G​(P)|=Dp′​(𝐍G​(P)).\displaystyle b(G)<\frac{|\mathrm{Irr}_{p^{\prime}}(G)|}{|G|}=\frac{|\mathrm{Irr}_{p^{\prime}}(\mathbf{N}_{G}(P))|}{|G|}\leq\frac{|\mathrm{Irr}_{p^{\prime}}(\mathbf{N}_{G}(P))|}{|\mathbf{N}_{G}(P)|}=D_{p^{\prime}}(\mathbf{N}_{G}(P)).

    If |𝐍G​(P)|<|G||\mathbf{N}_{G}(P)|<|G|, then 𝐍G​(P)\mathbf{N}_{G}(P) satisfies the conclusion of the theorem by the minimality of |G||G|. But this is a contradiction since b⁡(G)=b⁡(𝐍G​(P))b(G)=b(\mathbf{N}_{G}(P)) depends only on the local subgroup 𝐍G​(P)\mathbf{N}_{G}(P). So we are left to consider the case that 𝐍G​(P)=G\mathbf{N}_{G}(P)=G. Now, every χ∈Irrp′​(G)\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}_{p^{\prime}}(G) restricted to PP must be a sum of linear characters of PP by Clifford’s theorem, so P′≤ker⁡χP^{\prime}\leq\ker\chi. This means we may consider χ\chi a character of G/P′G/P^{\prime}, and so |Irrp′​(G)|≤|Irr⁡(G/P′)||\mathrm{Irr}_{p^{\prime}}(G)|\leq|\mathrm{Irr}(G/P^{\prime})|. Conversely, since P/P′P/P^{\prime} is an abelian normal subgroup of G/P′G/P^{\prime}, we have for all χ∈Irr⁡(G/P′)\chi\in\mathrm{Irr}(G/P^{\prime}) that χ⁡(1)\chi(1) divides [G/P′:P/P′]=[G:P][G/P^{\prime}:P/P^{\prime}]=[G:P] by Itô’s Theorem [22, Theorem 6.15]. So lifting χ\chi to a character of GG yields an irreducible character of p′p^{\prime}-degree. Hence, |Irrp′​(G)|=|Irr⁡(G/P′)|=k⁡(G/P′)|\mathrm{Irr}_{p^{\prime}}(G)|=|\mathrm{Irr}(G/P^{\prime})|=k(G/P^{\prime}).

    Now we work in the quotient G/P′=G¯=P¯⋊H¯G/P^{\prime}=\overline{G}=\overline{P}\rtimes\overline{H}, which has a normal, abelian Sylow pp-subgroup P¯\overline{P}. Note that Φ⁡(P¯)​⊴​G¯\Phi(\overline{P})\trianglelefteq\overline{G}, being characteristic in P¯​⊴​G¯\overline{P}\trianglelefteq\overline{G}. Moreover, CH¯​(P¯)​⊴​G¯C_{\overline{H}}(\overline{P})\trianglelefteq\overline{G}: it is normalized by H¯\overline{H} since P¯​⊴​G¯\overline{P}\trianglelefteq\overline{G}, and it is centralized, hence normalized, by P¯\overline{P}; so it is normal in G¯=P¯​H¯\overline{G}=\overline{P}\,\overline{H}. Recall that if N¯​⊴​G¯\overline{N}\trianglelefteq\overline{G}, then k⁡(G¯)≤k⁡(N¯)​k​(G/N¯)k(\overline{G})\leq k(\overline{N})k(\overline{G/N}) by [11]. Letting N¯=Φ⁡(P¯)​𝐂H¯​(P¯)\overline{N}=\Phi(\overline{P})\mathbf{C}_{\overline{H}}(\overline{P}) so that |N¯|=|Φ⁡(P¯)|​|𝐂H¯​(P¯)||\overline{N}|=|\Phi(\overline{P})||\mathbf{C}_{\overline{H}}(\overline{P})|, these being a pp-group and a p′p^{\prime}-group, and using the obvious inequality k⁡(N¯)≤|N¯|k(\overline{N})\leq|\overline{N}|, we then have

    k⁡(G¯)≤|𝐂H¯​(P¯)|⋅|Φ⁡(P¯)|⋅k⁡(P¯/Φ⁡(P¯)⋊H¯/𝐂H¯​(P¯)).\displaystyle k(\overline{G})\leq|\mathbf{C}_{\overline{H}}(\overline{P})|\cdot|\Phi(\overline{P})|\cdot k(\overline{P}/\Phi(\overline{P})\rtimes\overline{H}/\mathbf{C}_{\overline{H}}(\overline{P})).

    Now, the coprime action of H¯/𝐂H¯​(P¯)\overline{H}/\mathbf{C}_{\overline{H}}(\overline{P}) on the elementary abelian group P¯/Φ⁡(P¯)\overline{P}/\Phi(\overline{P}) is faithful by a coprime action theorem [23, Corollary 3.30]; so k⁡(P¯/Φ⁡(P¯)⋊H¯/𝐂H¯​(P¯))≤|P¯/Φ⁡(P¯)|k(\overline{P}/\Phi(\overline{P})\rtimes\overline{H}/\mathbf{C}_{\overline{H}}(\overline{P}))\leq|\overline{P}/\Phi(\overline{P})| by the k⁡(G​V)k(GV) theorem [12]. Additionally, H¯≅H\overline{H}\cong H since P′∩H=1P^{\prime}\cap H=1. Altogether, we then finally have that

    |Irrp′​(G)|=k⁡(G/P′)≤|𝐂H​(P/P′)|​|P/P′|.\displaystyle|\mathrm{Irr}_{p^{\prime}}(G)|=k(G/P^{\prime})\leq|\mathbf{C}_{H}(P/P^{\prime})|\,|P/P^{\prime}|.

    But then upon dividing through by |G|=|P|​|H||G|=|P||H|, we find that

    Dp′​(G)≤|P/P′|​|𝐂H​(P/P′)||P|​|H|=b⁡(G),\displaystyle D_{p^{\prime}}(G)\leq\frac{|P/P^{\prime}||\mathbf{C}_{H}(P/P^{\prime})|}{|P||H|}=b(G),

    a contradiction. ∎

    As a corollary, we deduce a criterion for detecting abelian Sylow pp-subgroups.

    Corollary 5.2.

    Let GG be a finite group, pp a prime and PP a Sylow pp-subgroup of GG. If Dp′​(G)>1/pD_{p^{\prime}}(G)>1/p, then PP is abelian. If, in addition, pp is the smallest prime dividing |G||G|, then GG has a normal pp-complement.

    Proof.

    By Theorem 5.1, 1/p<Dp′​(G)≤b⁡(G)1/p<D_{p^{\prime}}(G)\leq b(G); that is, p>|P′|[H:𝐂H(P/P′)]p>|P^{\prime}|[H:\mathbf{C}_{H}(P/P^{\prime})]. Therefore, |P′|=1|P^{\prime}|=1 and [H:𝐂H(P)]<p[H:\mathbf{C}_{H}(P)]<p. In particular, PP is abelian. If, in addition, pp is the smallest prime dividing |G||G|, then [H:𝐂H(P)]=1[H:\mathbf{C}_{H}(P)]=1. Therefore, P≤𝐙​(𝐍G​(P))P\leq\mathbf{Z}(\mathbf{N}_{G}(P)), and so GG has a normal pp-complement by Burnside’s transfer theorem [23, Theorem 5.13]. ∎

    This criterion is best possible since an extraspecial pp-group PP of order p1+2​mp^{1+2m} has p2​mp^{2m} representations of degree 11 and p−1p-1 irreducible representations of degree pmp^{m}. Therefore, |Irrp′​(P)|=p2​m|\mathrm{Irr}_{p^{\prime}}(P)|=p^{2m}, so Dp′​(P)=1/pD_{p^{\prime}}(P)=1/p and PP is not abelian.
